params.tau_out_desc: Time constant defining the speed of repolarization (return to rest).

params.tau_close_desc: Time for the h-gate to close (inactivation during plateau).

modals.ms_desc_base: The Mitchell-Schaeffer model describes action potential propagation using a potential variable (v) and a gate variable (h), simplifying ionic currents.
modals.minimal_desc_base: The Minimal Model is a 4-variable model that accurately reproduces restitution characteristics and spiral wave dynamics of human cardiac tissue.

basic.title: Understanding the 2D simulation - Mitchell-Schaeffer
basic.desc: This is the section dedicated to spatial simulations. Unlike the other simulations, here we work with a representation of the cardiac tissue. This allows us to see how electrical stimuli travel through the cells and create beat waves. In this representation, the Mitchell-Schaeffer model is used to simulate the electrical reactions.

basic.title: Understanding the 2D simulation - Minimal Model
basic.desc: This is the section dedicated to spatial simulations. Unlike the other simulations, here we work with a representation of the cardiac tissue. Unlike simplified models, with the Minimal Model we can better represent the behavior of the real heart, allowing us to identify the formation of reentry waves and identify reentry patterns.

math.title: The Math Behind 2D
math.cell_desc: At the cellular level, the Minimal Model uses four complete equations to independently manage the sodium, calcium, and potassium currents in human tissue:

basic.view_potential: The 'Transmembrane Potential' shows the wave traveling in real-time. You can click anywhere on the video to open an exact line graph of that point.
basic.view_lat: The 'Local Activation Time' uses colors to indicate when the wave arrived at each location. Dark blue is where the wave started, and dark red shows where it arrived last.
basic.view_apd: The 'Action Potential Duration' shows how long each piece of tissue took to relax after beating.
basic.stimuli_desc: You can add as many stimuli as you want to the tissue. Just choose whether it will be in the shape of a square or a circle, specify the position it should stimulate (X and Y coordinates), and at what point in time. Using two stimuli at different times is the classic way to create spiral waves.

advanced.title: Advanced Physiology and Arrhythmias
advanced.desc: In this section, you will discover how to simulate real problems and characteristics of cardiac tissue to create disease-prone environments.
advanced.tissue_desc: The heart does not have equal conductivity in all directions. It consists of fibers where electricity travels much faster in the longitudinal direction (Sigma_L) than in the transverse direction (Sigma_T). Changing the angle shifts the direction of these fibers, causing the wave to take on oval rather than circular shapes.
advanced.fibrosis_desc: Fibrosis is the formation of non-conductive scar tissue in the heart. It acts as an electrical insulator that blocks or diverts the propagation of the action potential, serving as one of the primary triggers for complex arrhythmias.
advanced.fib_compact: Shows a solid scar (round or square) at a defined position. The electrical wave will be forced to navigate around this obstacle, creating conduction delays.
advanced.fib_diffuse: Instead of a solid block, it scatters small points across a chosen area. This is a leading cause of Fibrillation, as these points break up the wavefront.
advanced.transmurality_desc: The muscular wall of the heart is composed of three distinct layers: Endocardium, Mid-myocardium (M-cells), and Epicardium. By enabling Transmurality, the simulator alters the action potential model used at each point in the tissue to reflect region-specific electrophysiological properties. This creates real heterogeneity in action potential duration (APD) and recovery times, allowing for the study of repolarization dispersion and arrhythmias.

math.diffusion_desc: The fundamental equation used is the diffusion equation. It states mathematically how energy is transferred from an excited cell to its empty neighbors:
math.numerical_desc: The simulation uses a square mesh where the position is calculated using 5-point neighborhoods in the Finite Difference Method. Spatial potential is solved by the Explicit Euler method, while the inactivation of cellular channels is solved by Rush-Larsen. Because many points are being calculated, this combination of methods, aligned with a multithreaded processing strategy, allows the simulation to run smoothly.

basic.title: What is the Mitchell-Schaeffer Model?
basic.desc: The Mitchell-Schaeffer model is a simplified representation of the electrical activity of a cardiac cell. Instead of calculating all individual ion currents (like sodium, potassium, and calcium), it groups this behavior into just two main variables: the membrane potential (cell Potential) and a 'gate' that controls the cell's resting period.
basic.why_use_desc: It is ideal for understanding fundamental concepts such as depolarization (contraction), repolarization (relaxation), and the refractory period (time the cell needs to recover before a new stimulus), requiring much less computational power than complex models.

advanced.title: Action Potential Dynamics
advanced.desc: In this model, the shape of the Action Potential (AP) is molded by the time constants ('Tau' parameters). By changing Tau_in, you modify the upstroke velocity of the AP. By changing Tau_out, you prolong or shorten the AP duration (APD).
advanced.gate_h_desc: The 'h' variable represents the availability of fast ion channels. When the cell is activated (V > V_gate), 'h' quickly drops to zero (governed by Tau_close), making the cell refractory. It only gradually recovers (governed by Tau_open) when the Potential drops below V_gate.
advanced.ref: Mitchell, C. C., & Schaeffer, D. G. (2003). A two-current model for the dynamics of cardiac membrane.

math.title: Mathematical Formulation
math.desc: The model is defined by a system of two coupled ordinary differential equations.
math.numerical_desc: Temporal integration is performed using a hybrid approach: the Explicit Euler method is used for the Potential variable (v), while the gate variable (h) is integrated using the Rush-Larsen method. The use of Rush-Larsen ensures high numerical stability for the opening and closing of the gate, as it uses an exact exponential solution for this step.

basic.title: What is the Minimal Model?
basic.desc: The Minimal Model (Bueno-Orovio Minimal Model) is an advanced simulation designed specifically to replicate human cardiac tissue. Unlike simpler models, it can highly accurately reproduce the realistic shape of the heartbeat in different parts of the heart.
basic.why_use_desc: The Minimal Model is useful for studying the behavior of cardiac cells under various conditions and for understanding the underlying mechanisms of heart rhythm.

advanced.title: Phenomenological Currents
advanced.desc: Instead of dozens of biological variables, the model uses 4 state variables (u, v, w, s) that control three main aggregated currents:
advanced.currents_list:
1. Fast inward current (J_fi): Responsible for rapid depolarization (phase 0).
2. Slow outward current (J_so): Controls repolarization and the plateau shape.
3. Slow inward current (J_si): Balances the plateau and interacts with implicit calcium dynamics.
advanced.ref: Bueno-Orovio, A., Cherry, E. M., & Fenton, F. H. (2008). Minimal model for human ventricular action potentials in tissue. Journal of theoretical biology, 253(3), 544-560.

math.title: System Equations
math.desc: The model calculates the evolution of the transmembrane potential (u) and three gating variables (v, w, s) through the following main equations:
math.numerical_desc: To ensure stability with reasonable time steps, the Potential variable (u) is integrated by the Explicit Euler Method, while the gate variables (v, w, s) use the Rush-Larsen method, which is ideal for linear differential equations of gating variables.

basic.title: What is the Ten Tusscher Model?
basic.desc: The Ten Tusscher model is a highly detailed electrophysiological representation of the human ventricle. Unlike 2-variable models, it uses 17 state variables, allowing precise analysis of ionic currents (sodium, potassium, calcium) and intracellular calcium dynamics.
basic.why_use_desc: Its main strength is the ability to simulate the effect of specific ionic channel blockades (e.g., calcium or sodium blockers) and understand how ionic homeostasis (Cai, Nai, Ki) behaves at different pacing frequencies.

advanced.title: Memory and Ionic Dynamics
advanced.desc: This model captures complex electrophysiological 'memory'. Ionic concentrations do not equilibrate instantaneously; they evolve with each beat, making the model ideal for studying arrhythmias caused by calcium overload or ionic imbalances.
advanced.ref: ten Tusscher, K. H., Noble, D., Noble, P. J., & Panfilov, A. V. (2004). A model for human ventricular tissue.

math.title: Mathematical Formulation
math.desc: The system solves 17 ODEs simultaneously. The potential V follows Ohm's law and capacitance, while ionic concentrations follow mass conservation and gate dynamics.
math.eq_ion: I_ion = IKr + IKs + IK1 + Ito + INa + IbNa + ICaL + IbCa + INaK + INaCa + IpCa + IpK
math.numerical_desc: The model uses Euler integration for ionic concentrations and Rush-Larsen for gating variables (x), ensuring numerical stability for the 17 simultaneous differential equations.

basic.title: Protocol: Multiple Stimuli (Mitchell-Schaeffer)
basic.desc: This protocol applies a train of consecutive pulses with a fixed Basic Cycle Length (BCL). It is essential for observing how the cardiac cell adapts to an imposed rhythm and verifying the stability of capture over time.
basic.why_use_desc: The 'BCL' (Basic Cycle Length) and 'No. of Stimuli' define the stress placed on the cell. If the BCL is shorter than the refractory period (governed by Tau_open), the cell will fail to respond to every stimulus, resulting in conduction blocks.

advanced.title: Advanced Dynamics & Alternans
advanced.desc: During rapid pacing (low BCL), the 'h' gate might not fully recover to its resting state between beats. This incomplete recovery can lead to alternans, where the action potential duration alternates between long and short beats.
advanced.gate_h_desc: The continuous pacing reveals the restitution properties of the model. The balance between Tau_out (repolarization) and Tau_open (recovery) dictates the minimum pacing frequency the cell can sustain.
advanced.ref: Mitchell, C. C., & Schaeffer, D. G. (2003). A two-current model for the dynamics of cardiac membrane.

math.title: Mathematical Formulation
math.desc: The underlying equations remain the same as the single stimulus, but the excitation current term (I_stim) is now a periodic function based on the BCL.
math.numerical_desc: Integration uses Explicit Euler for the Potential and Rush-Larsen for the gate variable, ensuring high stability over thousands of iterations during the repetitive pacing protocol.

basic.title: Protocol: Multiple Stimuli (Minimal Model)
basic.desc: Subjects the Minimal Model to a continuous pacing frequency. This is vital for analyzing the accumulation of slow variable inactivation and observing how human cardiac tissue adapts its Action Potential Duration (APD) in a steady state.
basic.why_use_desc: The 'BCL' heavily influences the stress and the final APD. Faster rhythms (lower BCL) naturally shorten the APD. Depending on the Cell Type (epi, endo, myo), this adaptation happens at different rates due to specific time constants for the outward and inward currents.

advanced.title: Rate Adaptation & Current Dynamics
advanced.desc: Rate adaptation in the Minimal Model is deeply connected to the slow recovery variables ('w' and 's').
advanced.currents_list: With consecutive pacing, the slow inward current (J_si) does not fully recover, progressively shortening the plateau phase. The 'myo' (M-cells) typically show a more pronounced APD prolongation at slow heart rates compared to 'epi' or 'endo' cells.
advanced.ref: Bueno-Orovio, A., Cherry, E. M., & Fenton, F. H. (2008). Minimal model for human ventricular action potentials in tissue.

math.title: System Equations
math.desc: The periodic application of external current acts as a continuous physiological perturbance to the 4-variable reaction system.
math.numerical_desc: Explicit Euler handles the Potential (u) while Rush-Larsen ensures high accuracy for the gating variables (v, w, s) throughout the repetitive pacing protocol.

basic.title: Protocol: Multiple Stimuli (Ten Tusscher)
basic.desc: Subjects the detailed Ten Tusscher model to a continuous pacing frequency. This allows observing the dynamic behavior and stabilization of intracellular ion concentrations.
basic.why_use_desc: The BCL dictates the pacing rate. Very fast rhythms (low BCL) prevent the sodium-potassium pump and calcium exchangers from re-establishing baseline levels, causing intracellular accumulation and affecting the action potential.

advanced.title: Long-Term Ionic Dynamics
advanced.desc: Full ionic models possess real 'memory'. The Ten Tusscher model needs dozens or hundreds of beats for intracellular calcium and the sarcoplasmic reticulum to enter thermodynamic equilibrium.
advanced.currents_list: During repetitive pacing, you can observe changes in the Calcium transient (Cai), which directly influences the simulated contraction force in electromechanical coupling.
advanced.ref: ten Tusscher, K. H., Noble, D., Noble, P. J., & Panfilov, A. V. (2004). A model for human ventricular tissue.

math.title: System Equations
math.desc: The system continuously solves the 17 ODEs at each pulse of the periodically applied stimulus current.
math.numerical_desc: Stability over long periods is guaranteed by integration methods tailored for gating variables (Rush-Larsen) and mass concentrations (Euler).

basic.title: S1-S2 Protocol
basic.desc: The S1-S2 protocol is a common simulation in computational and experimental cardiology. It consists of applying a sequence of regular stimuli (S1) to stabilize the cell in a continuous regular beating state. After this stabilization, a single premature stimulus (S2) is injected. The time interval between the last S1 and S2 (coupling interval) is progressively shortened until the cell stops responding. This lack of response maps the physiological limit of the cell.
basic.goal_desc: The primary goal of this protocol is to find the Effective Refractory Period (ERP): the shortest time interval in which the tissue can still mount a second action potential. If the S2 stimulus is delivered during the ERP, the channels responsible for depolarization will still be blocked (inactive) and the cell's response will be null, resulting in what we call loss of capture.

advanced.title: Recovery Dynamics and the Role of the 'h' Gate
advanced.desc: Despite having only two variables, the Mitchell-Schaeffer model accurately portrays the 'all-or-nothing' dynamics of cardiac cells. Excitability is entirely determined by the 'h' gate variable. During the action potential plateau generated by the S1 stimuli, the Potential is high, causing the value of 'h' to decay exponentially to near zero, reflecting the closing (inactivation) of the ion channels.
advanced.kinetics: The Kinetics of Refractoriness (Tau_open and Tau_close)
advanced.kinetics_desc: When the cell begins to repolarize and the transmembrane Potential falls below the threshold (V_gate), the 'h' gate begins its recovery towards 1 (fully open state) at a rate controlled by Tau_open. If the S2 stimulus is applied too early, the 'h' gate may not have recovered enough for the inward current flow to overcome the outward current, resulting in a block. Changing Tau_open directly prolongs or shortens the length of the Effective Refractory Period.
advanced.ref: Mitchell, C. C., & Schaeffer, D. G. (2003). A two-current model for the dynamics of cardiac membrane.

math.title: Computational Formulation and Resolution
math.desc: In the system's formulation, the extra stimulus (S2) is introduced into the ODEs through a pulse in the external current variable (I_stim), applied at time T_s2 = (N_s1 * BCL_S1) + BCL_S2.
math.stim_term: Where BCL_S2 is the variable coupling interval tested in this simulation.
math.numerical_desc: To ensure the stability of the model, we use a hybrid numerical approach. The differential equation governing the transmembrane Potential (v) is solved by the Explicit Euler method. In contrast, the inactivation variable (h) is integrated by the Rush-Larsen method, which solves the linear part of the ODE exactly, providing unconditional stability against abrupt transitions that would normally cause instability or explosion of accumulated error in the time steps.

basic.title: S1-S2 Protocol
basic.desc: Applying the S1-S2 protocol to the Minimal Model allows investigating how human ventricular tissue responds to premature beats. The model accommodates the complexities of four interconnected variables to accurately mirror the true time window in which heart muscle cells recover the ability to propagate a flawless pulse.
basic.goal_desc: In clinical practice, this protocol is employed during electrophysiological studies to quantify a patient's vulnerability to arrhythmias. Extremely early S2 intervals may not fail entirely, but trigger depressed and sluggishly conducting wavefronts. In real 2D or 3D tissues, these fronts are the classic triggers for the development of spiral waves and fibrillation episodes.

advanced.title: Interaction Between Multiple Gates
advanced.desc: Unlike the single blocking variable approach, refractoriness in the Minimal Model emerges from the competition between fast inactivation ('v' variable, analogous to sodium) and slow inactivation ('w' and 's' variables, representing calcium and potassium).
advanced.kinetics_desc: For a premature S2 pulse to be successful in creating a new potential, the system requires the availability of both the fast inward current (J_fi) and the slow inward current (J_si). If the Tau_v_minus or Tau_w_minus constant is lengthened by the user, the recycling of these critical currents after the end of the S1 beat will suffer severe delays. This accumulation of inactivation exponentially stretches the ERP barrier and flattens the magnitude of the depolarization phase if an S2 is applied at the limit of the stimulable window.
advanced.ref: Bueno-Orovio, A., Cherry, E. M., & Fenton, F. H. (2008). Minimal model for human ventricular action potentials in tissue.

math.title: Coupling and Numerical Precision
math.desc: The four state equations of the Minimal Model merge the contributions of the summed currents (J_fi, J_so, and J_si). The instantaneous injection of the S2 stimulus serves as a final test for the system. The stimulus will only cause reentry if the vector of the three gating variables (v, w, s) is properly conditioned and outside their respective inactivation values.
math.stim_term: The nonlinear response to the stimulus obeys a function present in the activation and inactivation terms of u.
math.numerical_desc: Due to the complexity of the Minimal Model, we use the Explicit Euler method to calculate the Potential (u). The control variables (v, w, s), on the other hand, are calculated by the Rush-Larsen method. This combination is perfect to keep the simulation stable and accurate, even when dealing with the short and fast stimuli of the S1-S2 protocol.

basic.title: S1-S2 Protocol (Ten Tusscher)
basic.desc: Applies the S1-S2 protocol to the detailed human Ten Tusscher model. This investigates how specific ionic currents (such as IKr, IKs, ICaL) recover to allow a premature beat.
basic.goal_desc: The S1-S2 test here maps not only the electrical refractory period but also the calcium transient refractory period. If S2 is applied prematurely, calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (CaSR) may fail or produce a much smaller peak.

advanced.title: Calcium Recovery Delay
advanced.desc: The L-type calcium current (ICaL) has slow recovery dependent on voltage and intracellular calcium. Closely coupled stimuli result in less calcium entry and thus shorter, weaker action potentials.
advanced.kinetics_desc: The temporary accumulation of sodium and calcium during the S1 sequence shifts the reversal potential, changing the driving force of repolarization currents. The S2 beat deals with this altered ionic landscape.
advanced.ref: ten Tusscher, K. H., Noble, D., Noble, P. J., & Panfilov, A. V. (2004).

math.title: Computational Evaluation
math.desc: The model resolves the extra stimulus (S2) by injecting the external current `I_stim` at the exact time, forcing the 17 variables to react outside their resting state.
math.stim_term: The Potential V response dynamically activates the gating variables m, h, j, xr1, xr2, xs, r, s, d, f.
math.numerical_desc: Due to the extreme stiffness of the Ten Tusscher model during abrupt depolarizations like S2, the Rush-Larsen method is fundamental to maintain stability.

restitution.what_is_desc: The restitution curve describes the relationship between the Action Potential Duration (APD) and the Diastolic Interval (DI). It is crucial for understanding cardiac stability and the mechanism of alternans.
restitution.what_is_for_desc: The restitution curve is a crucial analytical tool for predicting the stability of the cardiac rhythm. If the slope of the curve is too steep (typically greater than 1), it indicates a strong propensity for developing cardiac alternans and transitioning into fibrillation.
restitution.apd_def: APD (Action Potential Duration): Time the cell remains depolarized.
restitution.di_def: DI (Diastolic Interval): Resting time between the end of an AP and the start of the next.

basic.title: Restitution Curve: S1-S2
basic.desc: This module builds the restitution curve using the classic S1-S2 protocol. A train of S1 beats stabilizes the cardiac tissue to create a baseline memory, followed by a single premature S2 stimulus. The resting interval (Diastolic Interval - DI) between the last S1 and S2 is reduced with each iteration of the test.
basic.goal_desc: The graph maps the Action Potential Duration (APD) of the S2 beat as a function of the preceding Diastolic Interval (DI). The slope of this curve dictates the electrical stability of the heart: very steep curves (slope > 1) create fertile ground for electrical alternans and transitions to fibrillation.

advanced.title: Isolating Short-Term Memory
advanced.desc: The classic S1-S2 protocol isolates the 'short-term memory' of the cardiac tissue, since the baseline pacing rate (BCL S1) is strictly kept constant during the S2 sweeping test.
advanced.kinetics_desc: By holding long-term memory (ion inactivation accumulation) constant in the background, the S1-S2 curve cannot accurately predict the stability of sustained rapid rhythms, such as real tachycardia where the baseline heart rate itself accelerates.
advanced.ref: Karma, A. (1994). Electrical alternans and spiral wave breakup in cardiac tissue. Chaos, 4(3), 461-472.

math.title: Automated Numerical Sweep
math.desc: The worker runs dozens of batch simulations. For each different S2 BCL, the algorithm integrates the full Mitchell-Schaeffer model, detects the exact upstroke time, and measures the duration until 90% repolarization (APD90).
math.stim_term: The automated extraction of these points eliminates the need to draw points manually analytically, but to validate the model...
math.numerical_desc: For Mitchell-Schaeffer models, we plot a dotted curve generated by the exact theoretical analytical formula for restitution alongside the simulated data. This overlap serves as real proof of the rigor and reliability of our numerical integration routines in Euler/Rush-Larsen.

basic.title: Modified Mitchell-Schaeffer (MMS)
basic.desc: This variation of the Mitchell-Schaeffer model focuses on correcting a mathematical flaw at high frequencies. The goal is to reproduce restitution curves that are more accurate and less prone to the immediate collapse observed in some simplified cardiac simulations.
basic.goal_desc: In the classic MMS, maximum APD and the slope of the restitution curve are locked together by the same parameter. By making the closing time (Tau_close) non-constant, MMS allows tuning the curve slope freely without ruining the cell's resting duration.

advanced.title: Controlling the Onset of Alternans
advanced.desc: The fact that APD_max and maximum curve slope were so mathematically tied was a terrible obstacle to generating stable spiral waves in 2D simulations. MMS cuts this mathematical rope.
advanced.kinetics_desc: The term responsible for recovering the cell's inactivation gains a fixed dependence (h_min). Physiologically, this flattens and stabilizes the S1-S2 curve at fast intermediate frequencies, ensuring robust study of slow calcium currents without blowing up the model with unrealistically steep curves.
advanced.ref: Tolkacheva, E. G., Schaeffer, D. G., Gauthier, D. J., & Krassowska, W. (2003). Condition for alternans and stability... Physical Review E, 67(3).

math.title: The New Gate Equation
math.desc: The ODE controlling excitability (gate h) gains dynamic asymptotes and smoothly varying constants. Potential continuously modulates the inactivation process, rather than being an 'on/off' trigger.
math.stim_term: The direct consequence is that the mathematical relationship (APD = function of DI) becomes severely more complex and nonlinear.
math.numerical_desc: In the application graph, the dotted line shows exactly the closed formula proposed by Tolkacheva. The perfect alignment of the computed points with the line proves that our numerical approximations rigorously reproduce the altered physics.

basic.title: Dynamic Restitution Curve
basic.desc: In the dynamic protocol, there is no 'premature beat'. The cell is forced to beat at a continuous, repetitive constant rate (BCL) until the Action Potential Duration (APD) stops changing and reaches full equilibrium (steady-state). Only then is the APD value recorded. Then, the BCL is reduced and the process repeats.
basic.goal_desc: This test captures the true long-term adaptation of the heart. It measures how ion channels adapt and suffer lasting exhaustion when operating under rapid repeated beats (like real tachycardia), something invisible in S1-S2.

advanced.title: The Alternans Bible
advanced.desc: The slope of the Dynamic Curve has proven to be a spectacularly more reliable parameter for predicting transition to Ventricular Fibrillation than the standard S1-S2 curve.
advanced.kinetics_desc: If a cell or tissue has strong 'slow memory' and takes a while to adapt currents, the dynamic restitution curve is often substantially flatter than the S1-S2 curve. This explains why real tissues resist certain arrhythmias more than conventional theoretical tests suggest.
advanced.ref: Cherry, E. M., & Fenton, F. H. (2004). Suppression of alternans and conduction blocks despite steep APD restitution.

math.title: Computationally Heavy Protocol
math.desc: The dynamic protocol requires computing thousands or tens of thousands of beats just to plot a single curve, as the algorithm must sweep and simulate N serial beats before saving the results of the last one.
math.stim_term: Ensuring the absence of transient oscillation before the measurement cut-off is essential.
math.numerical: The Need for the Precise Method
math.numerical_desc: When computing repeated rhythms for very large continuous periods, simple Euler methods would accumulate error dust and produce non-stationary, jagged results. Using semi-implicit or piece-wise analytical methods (Rush-Larsen) on dependent variables ensures no 'leakage' occurs and the mathematical steady-state exactly mirrors biological reality.

basic.title: Restitution in Human Tissue (Minimal)
basic.desc: Using this module draws the complex restitution curve generated by the intricate 4-variable human model. Unlike phenomenological generalist formulations (Mitchell-Schaeffer), restitution here changes dramatically according to biological selection (Epicardial, Endocardial, or 'M-cells').
basic.goal_desc: Real Minimal Model curves are full of idiosyncrasies (biphasic, curves that flatten and suddenly drop). Detecting the point where APD falls into free fall is the exact window where premature beats tend to trigger spiral wavefronts (reentry).

advanced.title: Transmurality and Curve Dispersion
advanced.desc: The 'Myo' (M-cells), present in the core of the heart wall, have incredibly long potentials at slow rhythms, but their restitution curve aggressively shortens and crosses those of other cells under fast beating.
advanced.kinetics_desc: Careful modeling shows the struggle between the recovery of fast inward inactivation (v) versus the sluggish turn-off of secondary currents (w, s). Under continuous fast pacing, this dance between constants deeply affects the tissue's own restitution.
advanced.ref: Bueno-Orovio, A., Cherry, E. M., & Fenton, F. H. (2008). Minimal model for human ventricular action potentials in tissue.

math.title: Fast Multi-State Solution
math.desc: Not being susceptible to simple algebraic simplification for a 2-line theoretical curve, plotting this model's restitution reflects the absolute calculations of the multivariable Euler/Rush-Larsen integration running in milliseconds.
math.stim_term: Where plateau coupling and repolarization time dynamically define the DI and the corresponding APD.
math.numerical_desc: Because fast sodium channels are embedded in the system, the user can select 'Conduction Velocity' mode at the top. This mode collects the peak of maximum dV/dt derivative (which scales directly with Wave Speed in real cardiac tissue), building the classic, useful, and revealing CV restitution graph used by clinicians.

basic.title: Ionic Restitution (Ten Tusscher)
basic.desc: This tab builds the APD vs DI restitution curve using the Ten Tusscher model. It reflects the true ionic complexity of human ventricular tissue.
basic.goal_desc: The generated restitution curve is not a phenomenological approximation. It naturally emerges from the interplay between potassium (IKr, IKs, IK1) and calcium (ICaL) over time.

advanced.title: Short and Long-Term Memory
advanced.desc: Unlike simpler models, Ten Tusscher exhibits both short-term memory (channel recovery) and long-term memory (ion accumulation).
advanced.kinetics_desc: The slope of the restitution curve in this model is crucial for validating alternans mechanisms. The Epi model, for example, has a more sensitive repolarization transition due to its different Gks and Gto conductances.
advanced.ref: ten Tusscher, K. H., Noble, D., Noble, P. J., & Panfilov, A. V. (2004).

math.title: Multi-Variable Resolution
math.desc: The graph plots the measure of APD90 (time to 90% repolarization) after numerical integration of the 17 differential equations during the variable intervals of the test.
math.stim_term: The DI is dictated by continuous S1-S2 coupling, and responses are extracted from each complete iterative simulation.
math.numerical_desc: Plotting this curve requires thousands of computational steps. Rush-Larsen integration ensures stability in phase 0, while APD measurement occurs by evaluating the actual voltage drop.

basic.title: Fundamental Concepts
basic.desc: The FitzHugh-Nagumo model is a simplification of the Hodgkin-Huxley model. It is essential for understanding how excitable cells (like neurons and cardiac cells) generate a pulse and, most importantly, how they need a resting time before the next firing.
basic.goal_desc: Unlike the Bistable model, the FHN has a recovery variable. This means that after being excited, the cell enters a 'refractory period' where it cannot be stimulated again. In the simulator, you will see that the wave has an inhibitory 'tail' that prevents it from traveling backward.

advanced.title: Dynamics and Tissue Topology
advanced.desc: The model uses two main variables: voltage (v) and a recovery variable (w). The interaction between them allows for simulating highly complex behaviors.
advanced.kinetics_desc: By adjusting parameters 'a' and 'b', you change the resting state. If the system is highly excitable, it can oscillate on its own (pacemaker behavior). If it is less excitable, it will only respond to external stimuli.
advanced.boundaries_desc: The simulation allows testing two initial conditions. 'Left Pulse' simulates a linear fiber with closed ends (Neumann boundary). 'Reentry' connects the start and end of the cable forming a ring (periodic boundary) and applies an initial asymmetry (unidirectional block), creating a wave that circles the ring infinitely.
advanced.ref: FitzHugh R. (1961). Impulses and physiological states in theoretical models of nerve membrane.

math.title: Model Equations
math.desc: The system is described by two coupled differential equations governing activation and inactivation/recovery.
math.methods_desc: The spatial part uses Finite Differences. For time integration, it is used the 4th-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) method, ensuring accuracy in coupling the 'v' and 'w' variables. It also includes dynamic 'dt' limitation to guarantee CFL stability.
math.stim_term: Where 'ε' (epsilon) defines the slow time scale of recovery relative to rapid activation.

basic.title: Fundamental Concepts
basic.desc: The Bistable model is the simplest representation of an excitable medium. It describes how an electrical disturbance (potential) propagates through a one-dimensional cable, such as a purified cardiac fiber.
basic.goal_desc: In this model, there is a critical threshold (alpha). If the stimulus is weak, the cell returns to rest. If it exceeds the threshold, a stable wave is generated and travels through the entire tissue. This is the basis of electrical communication in the heart.

advanced.title: Wavefront Dynamics
advanced.desc: Unlike more complex models, the Bistable focuses on wavefront stability. It demonstrates how diffusion (Sigma) and local reaction interact to keep the wave shape constant during propagation.
advanced.kinetics_desc: The threshold parameter (alpha) defines excitability. If the threshold is too high or the conductivity is too low, the wave can undergo 'extinction' or conduction block, simulating failures that occur in diseased or ischemic tissues.
advanced.ref: Keener, J., & Sneyd, J. (1998). Mathematical Physiology. Springer.

math.title: Equation and Resolution
math.desc: The model is governed by a reaction-diffusion Partial Differential Equation (PDE) with a non-linear cubic term.
math.methods_desc: We use the Finite Difference Method for spatial discretization (Laplacian) and the 4th-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) method for time integration. The algorithm also implements an automatic check of the CFL condition, dynamically reducing the time step (dt) if its relationship with the spatial step (dx) exceeds the limit of numerical stability.

basic.title: Fundamental Concepts
basic.desc: The Mitchell-Schaeffer model is a representation focused specifically on cardiac muscle cells. Unlike simplified models, it accurately reproduces the real shape of an Action Potential, capturing the rapid depolarization phase followed by a long sustained plateau.
basic.what_is_1d_desc: Unlike a single isolated cell simulation (0D), a one-dimensional (1D) model arranges cells in a line, simulating a 'cable' or fiber of cardiac tissue. This allows us to observe not only the shape of the wave but also how electricity propagates across physical space.
basic.goal_desc: The main goal of this simulation is to analyze how an electrical signal physically moves along a cardiac fiber. You can observe the wavefront formation, the pulse width, and how the refractory period travels through space, which are essential features for understanding healthy electrical conduction.

advanced.title: Kinetics and Visualization
advanced.desc: This model groups the ion channels into two major forces: a rapid depolarizing inward current and a slow repolarizing outward current.
advanced.kinetics_desc: You can shape the wave duration by adjusting the Tau variables. 'Tau_in' controls the upstroke speed; 'Tau_out' dictates the duration of the fall and the plateau; and 'Tau_open/close' define the channel inactivation memory. The 'gate' parameter is the cutoff voltage that toggles between channel opening and closing.
advanced.visualizations_desc: The page offers two ways to analyze propagation: the 'Line Chart', which shows the amplitude of the potential (v) and the inactivation gate (h) along the cable at an exact instant in time; and the 'Spatiotemporal Chart' (Color Map), which maps the complete evolution of the wave, showing time on the vertical axis and position on the horizontal axis.
advanced.modes_desc: The simulation allows you to adjust structural parameters such as the cable length (L) and the spatial step (dx). The interaction between the local cellular current and spatial diffusion determines the speed and stability with which the wavefront advances through the simulated tissue.
advanced.ref: Mitchell, C. C., & Schaeffer, D. G. (2003). A two-current model for the dynamics of cardiac membrane.

math.title: Model Equations
math.desc: The system is governed by the transmembrane voltage (v) and a single cellular inactivation gate (h) that controls the rapid inward current.
math.methods_desc: To ensure maximum stability and accuracy, a hybrid solution is used. In time, it applies Explicit Euler for the voltage diffusion (v), but for the state variable (h) it uses the Rush-Larsen method. The simulator also features active protection by dynamically limiting the integration step according to the CFL condition.
math.stim_term: The conditional equation for 'h' acts as a switch that decouples the depolarization phase from the repolarization phase.

basic.title: What is the Restitution Curve?
basic.desc: The Restitution Curve shows how the propagation speed of the action potential adapts in response to different heart rates.
basic.goal_desc: Evaluate the electrical stability of the tissue by simulating the S1-S2 protocol, allowing the identification of conditions that lead to arrhythmias. Furthermore, analyzing the slope of the curve is essential, as slopes greater than 1 are classic indicators of instability and electrical alternans.

advanced.title: S1-S2 Protocol in 1D
advanced.desc: The protocol applies a train of stimuli (S1) with a constant basic cycle length (BCL) to reach a steady state, followed by a premature stimulus (S2).
advanced.visualizations_desc: You can plot the Conduction Velocity (CV) against the Coupling Interval (CI) or the Diastolic Interval (DI). The DI more directly reflects the recovery time of ion channels.

math.title: Velocity Calculation (CV)
math.desc: Conduction Velocity is calculated by dividing the physical distance by the difference in activation time between two points on the cable.

basic.title: Fundamental Concepts
basic.desc: The 'Source-Sink Mismatch' phenomenon is a central principle in electrophysiology. It occurs when an electrical wave must pass from a narrow region of tissue (the 'Source', which generates current) to a much wider region (the 'Sink', which must be charged/excited by the current).
basic.goal_desc: In this simulator, the wave travels through an isthmus (a slit). Upon exiting the slit and hitting the open tissue, the wavefront expands drastically. If the slit is too narrow, the few cells of the 'source' cannot provide enough electrical charge to excite the huge amount of cells in the 'sink', causing an abrupt block where the wave simply 'dies'.

advanced.title: Anisotropy and Obstacles
advanced.desc: This 2D model allows testing conduction failure under real adverse conditions. Cardiac tissue has fibers, meaning electricity travels faster in one direction (longitudinal) than the other (transverse).
advanced.kinetics_desc: You can add compact or diffuse fibrosis. The algorithm supports 'Border Zones', where conductivity smoothly decays at the periphery of the scar (using linear interpolation), reproducing the heterogeneity of real infarct borders.
advanced.models_desc: The page allows toggling between the Mitchell-Schaeffer model and the Minimal Model. This allows comparing how different calcium and potassium dynamics resist the same anatomical barrier.
advanced.ref: Kléber, A. G., & Rudy, Y. (2004). Basic mechanisms of cardiac impulse propagation and associated arrhythmias.

math.title: Equations and Diffusion Tensor
math.desc: To compute fiber direction, the traditional spatial Laplacian is replaced by a two-dimensional Anisotropic Diffusion Tensor.
math.methods_desc: For spatial discretization, the worker uses the Central Finite Difference Method. In time, integration uses Euler for voltage and the Rush-Larsen method for gating variables. The dynamic 'dt' calculation (CFL) relies on the maximum diffusion tensor to prevent instabilities.
math.stim_term: Dxx, Dyy, and Dxy are the coefficients derived from the sigma_L, sigma_T velocities and the fiber angle.

export_modal.title: Export Simulation
export_modal.subtitle: Select the desired format for download.
export_modal.png_desc: Saves the exact current view of the simulation chart.
export_modal.data_desc: Exports raw values for advanced analysis in software like ParaView.
export_modal.gif_desc: Generates a short looping video of the temporal simulation.
